Layer: domain
Feature state: active
Review lane: cleanup
Files:
- packages/execution-engine/src/workers/disk-headroom-reclaim.ts
- packages/app/src/delete-all-snapshot.ts
- packages/execution-engine/src/workers/reaper-reclaim.ts
- packages/execution-engine/src/__tests__/reaper-reclaim.test.ts
Change types:
- modify
- modify
- create
- create
Acceptance criteria:
- An entry matching the existing dot-deleting naming convention, older than thirty minutes, is removed locally and on a configured remote target; a fresh one of the same name is left alone.
- An immediate child of either known automation-checkout location, older than forty-eight hours, is removed; a fresh one, and the location itself, are left alone.
- Calling the third check with a pile larger than the configured limit trims it to exactly that limit.
- A known log file larger than the configured size limit is rewritten to keep only its most recent portion; a small one is left alone.
- `cd packages/execution-engine && pnpm test` and `cd packages/app && pnpm test` both exit 0.
Goal: Add four independent cleanup checks -- one per category of accumulating disk waste found this session -- to one new module, each removing or trimming only what its own narrow, already-established naming or age convention identifies.
Motivation: Traced directly against real production waste this session. An orphaned dot-deleting entry only ever gets removed as a side effect of a critical-disk-pressure cleanup that a host sitting below that line never triggers. Two automation-checkout locations accumulate per-item work with nothing ever removing old items. A snapshot-retention limit already exists and already works, but only ever runs at the tail of snapshot creation, so a snapshot attempt that never reaches that point leaves the pile to keep growing past its own configured limit. A known set of log files has no size limit anywhere in this codebase.
Alternative considerations: Considered leaving the dot-deleting sweep folded only inside the existing critical-only cleanup. Rejected because that is exactly the gap that let a real 14GB orphan sit unremoved indefinitely on a host that never crossed the critical line. Considered re-deriving the snapshot-retention limit as a second, independent number in the new module. Rejected in favor of calling the two existing functions that already resolve and enforce that exact limit, so there is only ever one definition of what the limit is.
Non-goals: This task does not add the interval-driven background process that calls these four checks on a schedule; that is the next task. It does not change any existing behavior of the two modified files beyond adding one export keyword to each; both already work correctly today and keep doing exactly what they already do for every other caller.
Implementation details:
1. In the existing disk-pressure reclaim file (see Files above), add the export keyword to its private name-matching helper for dot-deleting entries, with no other change to that file, so the new module can reuse it instead of duplicating the same one-line check.
2. In the existing snapshot file (see Files above), add the export keyword to its private function that resolves the configured retention count, with no other change to that file, so the new module can reuse it instead of hardcoding a second number.
3. Add a new file with four independent functions. The first reaches the local machine and every configured remote target the same way the existing disk-pressure checks already do, and removes any entry matching the existing dot-deleting naming convention once it is older than thirty minutes, running only that narrow removal and not the broader wipe the existing critical-disk-pressure cleanup already performs.
4. The second removes any immediate child of two known automation-checkout locations once that child is older than forty-eight hours, leaving the two locations themselves untouched.
5. The third calls the two now-exported functions from steps 1 and 2 together, directly, on this new module's own schedule, so the existing retention limit is enforced even on a run where the path that is supposed to enforce it after each snapshot does not reach that step.
6. The fourth keeps only the most recent portion of a known set of log files once any one of them grows past a size limit, rewriting the file in place rather than removing it outright.
7. Add tests for all four functions in one new test file, covering an entry old enough to be acted on and one too recent to be touched, for each of the four.
Review claim: Approve four independent cleanup checks, one per category of accumulating disk waste found this session, added to one new module, each removing or trimming only what its own narrow, already-established naming or age convention identifies.
Safety invariant: Every check only acts on an entry matching a specific, narrow naming or age convention already established elsewhere in this codebase or defined in this same task; nothing outside those exact conventions is touched, and the two existing files only gain one export keyword each with no other change to their current behavior.
Slice rationale: Kept as one task because all four checks are the same kind of change -- add a narrowly scoped removal or trim to one new module -- and three of the four reuse an existing, already-tested convention or function rather than inventing new logic, so reviewing them together is reviewing one small module, not four unrelated ones.
Architectural effect: Adds one new module holding four independent cleanup functions; two existing files each gain one export keyword with no behavior change. No existing caller of either modified file changes.

Acceptance criteria:
- The new background process calls each of the four functions from the prior task once per interval.

Goal: Add one new interval-driven background process that calls the four checks from the prior task on a repeating schedule, added to the existing list of background processes this application already starts the same way its nearest sibling already is.
Motivation: The four checks from the prior task need something that calls them periodically, independent of any disk-pressure threshold, so they run as steady-state hygiene rather than only in response to an emergency. This application already has an established shape for exactly this kind of background process.
Alternative considerations: Considered folding these four checks into the existing critical-only disk-pressure background process. Rejected because that process's own trigger is exactly the gap this plan closes -- it only acts at a pressure threshold a host may never reach, and its own cooldown is tuned for emergency response, not hourly hygiene.
Non-goals: This task does not change what any of the four checks themselves do; it only calls them on a schedule. It does not change the existing critical-only disk-pressure background process at all.
Implementation details:
1. Add a new file that builds one interval-driven background process the same way the nearest existing sibling of this kind already does, calling each of the four functions from the prior task once per interval, a default of one hour apart.
2. Give this new background process the same kind of record-keeping entry the nearest existing sibling already writes on each pass, so what it did is visible in the same place other background processes already report to.
3. Add this new background process to the existing list of background processes this application already starts, the same way its nearest sibling is already present in that same list.
4. Add tests for this new file following the same style already used for testing its nearest sibling, injecting the four functions from the prior task and confirming a single pass calls each one and writes one record-keeping entry.
Review claim: Approve one new interval-driven background process that calls the four checks from the prior task on a repeating schedule, added to the existing list of background processes this application already starts.
Safety invariant: This only adds a new background process and one new entry to an existing list; no existing background process, including the critical-only disk-pressure one, changes at all.
Slice rationale: Kept separate from the checks themselves because this task only wires an existing pattern for starting a background process around functions that already exist once the prior task lands; nothing here changes what any individual check does.
Architectural effect: The application gains one more background process running on its own schedule; no existing background process's behavior changes.
